newsitem.title: UK: Halifax vote to go ahead despite criticism.
newsitem.headline: Halifax vote to go ahead despite criticism.

text.p: The Halifax, Britain's largest building society, said on Thursday it intended to go ahead with Monday's vote on its 11 billion pound ($17.8 billion) flotation despite continuing controversy over the terms of the scheme.
The plans have been widely attacked for paying bonuses only to first-named account members. As a result the elderly, disabled or children who have accounts held in trust will miss out on the payouts.

Conservative member of parliament, Douglas French, has brought a private members' bill designed to prevent the exclusion of beneficiaries of trustee accounts in the future. He has also called on Halifax to consider a voluntary payout to compensate those missing out.

The Halifax rejected the proposals and said the re-documentation needed for such a move would delay bonus payments likely to average around 1,300 pounds for its 8.5 million members for at least a year.

"Mr French suggests that the bill should be adopted by us on a voluntary basis. That's not possible without us going back to the drawing board and sending out another transfer document and getting another vote going which we don't intend to do," said a spokesman for the Halifax.
"Our meeting is on Monday. We don't want to delay the process by 12 months or so which is what is implied by starting again."
The Halifax again defended its existing scheme, arguing that it linked share benefits to voting membership which, it said, reflected the principle of mutuality in a fair way.
It said it did not keep a record of people named second on accounts because they "were not members of the Halifax".
As it stands the bill -- the Building Societies (Distributions) Bill -- applies only to societies which announce plans to convert after January 22, 1997.
The possibility of the bill being made retrospective by an amendment in the House of Lords was dismissed as very unlikely by the Halifax.

"If it was made retrospective -- which is very unlikely given the nature of a 10 minute rule bill which often don't go through and more rarely go through with amendments -- it would almost certainly mean a 12 month delay," said the Halifax spokesman.
The bill is due to go to the Lords on February 28.

The result of the Halifax's vote will be declared after a special general meeting in Sheffield on Monday. Half of the Halifax's savers must vote with three-quarters in favour of the scheme to be approved. ($1=.6184 Pound)
